## Part A - Arithmetic Operations and Basic Data Types

```{r}
a <- 17
b <- 5

print(a + b)
print(a - b)
print(a * b)
print(a / b)

print(a %/% b)
print(a %% b)

print(2 ^ 10)

print(17 / 5)
print( 17 %% 5)
print(17 %/% 5)

print (10 %% 3)
print(10 %/% 3)
```
1. Imagine sharing 17 cookies equally among 5 friends
17 %/% 5 - Each friend gets 3 whole cookies. 
17 %% 5 - You have 2 cookies left over in the box
17 / 5 - If you slice up those 2 leftovers, everyone gets 3.4 cookies total.

2. I predicted the of 10 %% 3 is 1 because this operator gives the remainder (modulo), I predicted the output will be 3 because this operator gives the whole number quotient. 

## Part B - Basic Data Types: typeof(), class(), and mode()

```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)

mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```
3. The x <- 42 is a double it can have decimal point but y <- 42L is an integer the 'L' instruct R that it is an integer, it can only store whole number. 

4. Yes, because typeof() reports how R physically stores the data behind the scenes like double or integer, while class() and mode() report how R labels and treats the object overall like numeric or factor. A factor's typeof() is "integer" because R stores categories as numbers behind the scenes, but its class() is factor, A matrix's typeof() is the data type inside it like "double", but its class() is matrix.

## Part C - Type Conversion
```{r}
num_string <- "123"
num_val <- as.numeric(num_string)
typeof(num_val)
class(num_val)
mode(num_val)

as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)

bad_string <- "hello123"
as.numeric(bad_string)
```
5. R uses a warning so long scripts or big datasets can keep running even if a few text values fail to convert. Unnoticed NA values will quietly pollute your dataset and lead to incorrect calculations or errors later on.

6. Both will produce TRUE. R converts 0 to FALSE, while any non-zero number is converted to TRUE.

##Part D - Strings, paste(), and paste0()
```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

print(first_name)
print(last_name)

full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)
full_name

paste0(first_name, last_name)

paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")

age <- 21
paste0(full_name, " is ", age, " years old.")
```
7. paste() automatically inserts a space between strings by default, whereas paste0() connects strings directly together with zero space in between.

8. No, it did not cause an error. paste0() automatically converts non-string values like age into text behind the scenes before joining them.

##Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
as.numeric("5") + 5
```
9. R requires explicit conversion to prevent silent errors and unintended bugs, ensuring the programmer actively decides whether data should be treated as text or numbers.

10. The column was likely imported as text instead of numbers, often caused by missing values or text headers in the file. To diagnose it, run typeof() or class() on the column to check its storage type. To fix it, convert the column using as.numeric(), while checking for warnings about NA values.

Conclusion: R stores data using specific storage types like double, integer, and character, where typeof() checks low-level memory storage and class() identifies how R treats the object overall. Understanding these distinctions is critical because R does not automatically convert text into numbers for math operations, leading to errors when types are mismatched. Using explicit conversion functions like as.numeric() allows us to safely prepare variables before doing arithmetic or joining strings. Inspecting types and handling conversions early prevents hidden NA values and ensures accurate, error-free analysis.
